full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I agree with the first pass, but the result is a trivial, built-in consequence of the rule, not a real emergent pattern.

**What the rule does.** There are two fixed node types (kN=2). On every step, every edge is rewired so that it ends on a node of the same type. The types never change, so this is a pure rewiring process. The graph can only stop changing once no edge joins two different types. At that point it must have split into at least one connected piece per type, so at least two components. The measured median of about 2.9 components, against about 1.5 in the knock-out, is what this design guarantees, plus a few leftover small or isolated pieces.

**Where it is documented.** This is the rewiring-only limit of the coevolving (adaptive) voter model:
- **Holme & Newman (2006)** combine opinion spreading with network connections forming *"between individuals of similar beliefs"*. One parameter sets the balance between the two processes. These models divide into two classes, those in which individuals form their beliefs based on the opinions of their neighbors in a social network of personal acquaintances, and those in which, conversely, network connections form between individuals of similar beliefs. Here we present a simple model of this combination, with a single parameter controlling the balance of the two processes.
- **Durrett et al., "Graph fission in an evolving voter model" (PNAS 2012)** use a two-opinion model with a discordant edge, meaning one that joins nodes with different opinions. With probability α that edge is broken and reconnected to an individual chosen at random (*i*) from those with the same opinion or (*ii*) from the network as a whole. Option (i) is the "rewire-to-same" rule, the same mechanism as REWIRE_SAME here. The evolution of the system stops when there are no longer any discordant edges connecting individuals with different opinions. The system here is the α=1 limit, where opinions never change. In that limit the final minority fraction equals the starting one (ρ ≈ u for α > αc) and the graph splits by type.
- The related nonlinear coevolving voter model describes a phase diagram that includes an absorbing phase in a fragmented network.

**Is it trivial or an artifact?** Yes, it is trivial. It is a frozen absorbing state that is fixed in advance: the end state is one cluster per type, and the rule writes that in directly. The count passes the knock-out test, holds up when the system is scaled, and is not a numerical failure. Still, nothing emerges beyond "edges sort themselves by type". The roughly 0.9 components above the floor of 2 probably come from isolated or small pieces left over from the starting graph. I could not find any twist in the behaviour (for example in how the components are sized, or how fast fission happens) that the fission literature does not already cover.

**Caveat.** The notation "N[0]" could mean that only type-0 nodes rewire. That changes nothing important: once the type-0 nodes drop their mixed-type edges, the same split happens.
